albums.blurb: El Ten Eleven are a Los Angeles duo — Kristian Dunn on a double-neck guitar/bass run through live looping pedals, and Tim Fogarty on drums — who build their layered pieces in real time with no backing tracks. This self-titled debut appeared on the tiny Fake Record Label in August 2004 and was reissued by Bar/None the following year; opener "My Only Swerving" remains their signature piece, and the duo's music later ran through Gary Hustwit's design documentaries Helvetica, Objectified and Urbanized.
albums.reception: Spin described the debut as "experimental instrumental music that's both highly skilled and deeply felt," likening the duo to "a sort of Silverlake-style Sigur Rós."

albums.blurb: Jack Stauber is an Erie, Pennsylvania songwriter and animator whose warped, VHS-grained stop-motion videos are inseparable from his songs. Pop Food, released in March 2017 on his own Plopscotch Records imprint, is his third album, a set of short synth-and-sample bedroom pop pieces with a 1980s home-video sheen; its first two tracks, "Buttercup" and "Oh Klahoma," are the ones that escaped into the wider internet.
albums.reception: "Buttercup" became a viral TikTok phenomenon and had passed 470 million Spotify streams as of March 2026.

albums.blurb: Kings of Convenience are the Bergen, Norway duo of Eirik Glambek Bøe and Erlend Øye, who sing in close two-part harmony over interlocking acoustic guitars. Quiet Is the New Loud, released on Astralwerks in January 2001, was their breakthrough: its title doubled as a manifesto for hushed chamber pop, and contemporary reviews reached repeatedly for Simon & Garfunkel comparisons. Øye later fronted The Whitest Boy Alive, and the duo followed with Riot on an Empty Street in 2004.
albums.reception: The album reached No. 1 in Norway, where it is certified Gold (it holds a Silver certification in the UK), and lent its name to the British music press's "New Acoustic Movement."
